payload.text:
STALENESS AUDIT (2026-09-14, read-only; nothing in the engine changed).

Prior runs and the versions they measured:
- R01–R04 resume bench: 0.1 to 0.5, Jul 8–11.
- S2-R01: 0.9.2. S2-R02: 0.10.0.
- Drift scenarios 3 and 4: 0.25.1, pricing and smoke runs only.
- Driver 4.1 proof: pre-release code, before the two driver bugs b065fc5 fixed for 0.30.0.
- Micro-perf pins: Jul 20 – Aug 8.
No run covers 0.31.0.

Claims with no current backing:
- "<2% drift": no graded run exists (scenario 3 had n=2 packets; scenario 4 stopped at task 4.1).
- "2.44M vs 5.80M billed tokens per task": one run against one hand-picked manual session.

Fixed per-session overhead, measured on the session-driver record by building 0.10.0 / 0.25.1 / 0.31.0 in the scratchpad:
- SessionStart digest: 6,129 / 8,574 / 8,574 bytes.
- MCP tool definitions: 7 / 10 / 12 tools, 4,130 / 9,728 / 14,179 characters (about 1.0k to 3.5k tokens, sent every turn).
- Protocol block that `sofar init` writes: 3,406 / 4,384 / 5,723 bytes.
- Total: about 2.5k tokens at 0.10.0, now about 5.6k, plus about 1.4k for the protocol block.
- Hook medians got FASTER (stop 55 → 24 ms). session-start is back up to 74 ms, likely the 0.26 shipping-notice git read (unconfirmed).
- Consequence: S2-R02's −32.1% cost result is the most stale; drift-certification is moderately stale; driver 4.1 is least stale.

PROPOSED BENCHMARK AREAS
- A0 Overhead footprint (deterministic, no model cost): digest bytes, tool-schema characters, protocol-block bytes, and hook/fold latency at 10 / 100 / 1000 initiatives. Pin it per release.
- A1 Cost: billed tokens per COMPLETED task, split into input, cache-write, cache-read and output, plus API-priced $. Plot it against task index to show the cost curve's shape.
- A2 Time: wall-clock per task; time and turns to the first productive edit (orientation latency); operator minutes and number of interventions.
- A3 Outcome: objective pass (tests and acceptance criteria) before grader scores; pass@1 plus pass^k consistency across k reps.
- A4 Continuity: re-explanation cost (M1), clarifying questions asked, recall probe (task 7; R02 W2 arm S was UNRECOVERABLE), and whether the session picks the correct next action.
- A5 Decision adherence: walked-into rate on rejected approaches and standing constraints (the <2% claim).
- A6 Grounding: fabricated paths, ids and decisions (R02: L 30% / S 21%).
- A7 Long-horizon degradation: quality and cost vs task index, and compaction events, for one long session vs fresh sessions.
- A8 Autonomy (`sofar drive`): tasks per run with no intervention, stall rate, needs_user precision, handoff-reason accuracy, recovery.
- A9 Portability: the same record and workload run through claude-code, codex and opencode.
- A10 Concurrency and integrity: parallel sessions, write-back collisions, zero log corruption.

BASELINES TO COMPARE AGAINST
- B0 Bare agent with no memory.
- B1 Agent plus a hand-maintained CLAUDE.md / AGENTS.md and a notes file (the realistic default).
- B2 One long session with auto-compaction (arm L).
- B3 Third-party memory/task layers, e.g. Cline Memory Bank, claude-mem, Beads, Task Master. Verify that each still exists before selecting it.

Existing benchmarks such as SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench score single-session task success. None scores cross-session continuity. So A3 is table stakes, and A4 through A8 are where sofar's claim lives.

Machinery to reuse from handoff-bench (session-strategy-bench rejected building a new bench): pre-registration, byte-identical workloads W1/W2 (W3 never run), equalized arms (the planned R03 fix for the skills asymmetry), graders A/B/C, the fabricated-path sidecar, and cell isolation from drift-certification.

LAUNCH-FIT REVIEW (2026-09-14): re-ranks the A0–A10 areas for a public launch (social, Product Hunt, website). Based on web pain research and the product docs.

PAIN RANKING (evidence → pay/switch signal)
1. Usage-limit / quota burn. Strongest switch signal: cancellations, moves to Codex, a class action (Jun 2026, expanded Sep 8). Sources: anthropics/claude-code#9424, openai/codex#30918, Engadget.
2. Almost-right output and review burden (SO 2025: 66% hit "almost right"; METR measured −19%). Drives non-adoption more than purchase.
3. Context lost across sessions or after /compact; re-explaining. #24460 was closed as not planned. claude-mem has 93.9k stars and Beads 27.1k. Install signal is high; pay signal is weak.
4. Agent ignores CLAUDE.md or past decisions. At least 6 bug reports Dec 2025–Mar 2026 (#15443, #22503, #27032, #34774).
5. Unattended runs drift and need babysitting (#28875).
6. Repeating rejected approaches. Anecdotal; rides on 3 and 4.
7. Hallucinated packages and paths. Rarely voiced as a pain now.
8. Parallel agents conflicting. Weak.
Subscription users feel cost as quota spent, not dollars. Report cost as headroom: % of the 5h window per task, tasks per week before the cap.

RE-TIER OF AREAS FOR PUBLIC USE
- Headline: A1 recast as limit headroom NET of sofar's own overhead; A4 resume without re-explaining, including a post-/compact scenario; A5 rejected approaches re-proposed vs a CLAUDE.md baseline; A8 interventions per N tasks under `sofar drive`.
- Guard (must show no regression): A3 outcome, scored objectively by tests, not LLM judges.
- Technical appendix: A0 overhead, hook latency, A6 grounding, A7 curves, A9 portability, A10 integrity.
- Reframe time: S2-R02 wall-clock went −10.7% / +52%, so wall-clock is not a safe claim. Operator attention minutes are (driver 4.1: 6 vs 78 min).

GAPS THE A-LIST MISSED
- G1 BASELINE: the bar to beat is CLAUDE.md plus Claude Code's built-in auto-memory, not a bare agent or one long session. HN top comment on a 225-comment memory Show HN (46426624): "nothing works better than simply keeping my own library of markdown files". Prior arm L was one long session, so no prior run answers this baseline.
- G2 OVERHEAD HONESTY: fixed injection is now ~7k tokens (tool schemas ~3.5k every turn, digest ~2.1k, protocol block ~1.4k). Publish the net figure and the break-even task length. Consider trimming the tool schemas before launch.
- G3 UPKEEP: minutes per week a developer spends curating the record, against a hand-kept markdown file.
- G4 TIME TO FIRST VALUE: install to first successful cold resume.
- G5 WRONG-MEMORY HARM: a stale or contradicted record. Is it caught (staleness and drift signals) or does it mislead? Critics will ask.
- G6 BUYER PROOF: the spine's buyer is the eng lead, not solo devs, who are "strong users, weak customers". Needs cross-tool handoff (Claude Code → Codex) and intent recoverability ("why was X built", answered from the record, time and accuracy).
- G7 ZERO-EGRESS PROOF: a network trace showing no model calls or egress. Differentiates from claude-mem, which calls a model to compress.

CREDIBILITY REQUIREMENTS (HN/X)
- A public workload repo. brillo-bench is private and unpublishable.
- A one-command reproducible harness.
- Multiple reps with confidence intervals.
- Fresh, uncontaminated tasks.
- Competitors configured fairly with configs published, or left out. This was the core of the mem0/Zep/Letta disputes.
- Losses shown, including R02 W2 recall UNRECOVERABLE and the wall-clock regressions.

LAUNCH-SIDE ISSUES
- The action plan holds PH and Show HN "until design partners validate onboarding" (product doc/02-sofar-action-plan.md:58-65).
- The one-pager's only numbers are R04 on ~0.3–0.5.
- The one-pager's install command says @alignlabs/sofar; the README says sofar.sh.
- The README says "adds nothing to your bill" next to `drive --cost-cap`.

payload.text:
WORKLOAD ASSESSMENT: Peak vs a fresh app (2026-09-14, read-only look at ~/IO/peak).

What Peak is today:
- github.com/jithinio/peak, visibility PRIVATE, 104 commits, last one 2026-06-08.
- A Next.js + bun + turbo monorepo (apps/web; packages auth, database, ui) with about 432 TS/TSX files.
- A frontend demo whose docs describe a real product (PropFlow architecture, database schema, wireframes).
- Depends on the PAID Hugeicons Pro private registry, via an .npmrc auth token.
- Already carries a .sofar record (initiative auth-backend).

Why Peak can't be the controlled, public benchmark:
- Outsiders can't reproduce it without a Hugeicons Pro token.
- Publishing the workload means open-sourcing a real product's code.
- Its existing .sofar record and CLAUDE.md contaminate the non-sofar arms, which would need purging.
- A controlled run builds the same tasks N times × 6 arms from one snapshot, which yields ~30+ divergent copies of Peak, not one shipped product.

RECOMMENDATION: use both, in different roles.
(a) CONTROLLED BENCHMARK: a fresh purpose-built public app, MIT-licensed, open dependencies only, SQLite (no infrastructure).
- Tasks: 25–30 across ~10 sessions, deliberately CHAINED. Later tasks depend on earlier choices: data model, auth approach, conventions, a rejected approach planted naturally. Without chaining, C5 quality can only show parity.
- Scoring: a hidden acceptance test suite written before run 1.
- Split into a TUNING task set and a HELD-OUT task set (D5).
- Suggested domain: something every judge understands, with real accumulating decisions, e.g. an invoicing / booking / issue-tracker app.
(b) REAL-WORLD CASE STUDY: build Peak fully WITH sofar as dogfood.
- Not a controlled comparison.
- Report record-derived numbers: sessions, tokens, interventions, handoffs.
- Feed every sofar failure seen there into the D5 loss study.
- Gives the launch a "we built a real product with it" story.
Awaiting the user's ruling.

payload.text:
PROPOSALS AWAITING USER RULING (2026-09-14). Nothing here is decided.

(A) PLAN-HEADROOM MINI-BENCHMARK. The user proposed "30–50% saved, $100/month from context alone".
Status: an UNMEASURED hypothesis. Prior evidence:
- S2-R01: −17.7%; S2-R02: −32.1% (API-priced, on 0.9.2/0.10.0, 6-task workloads).
- Driver 4.1: −58% (2.44M vs 5.80M billed tokens per task), but n=1 on pre-release code.
- Fixed injection has since grown ~2.1x.
So 30–50% goes into the pre-registration as a PREDICTION, never as copy.
Proposed output, a cut of the C1 runs, per plan:
- Claude $100 and $200 plans: % of weekly limit per chain, extra tasks per week. The dollar framing is valid only as "stay on $100 instead of upgrading to $200".
- Codex under a ChatGPT subscription: % of its limit.
- Cursor (usage/credit-billed): real $ per task.
- OpenCode via API: real $ per task.
Limits are not published in tokens, so each plan's own usage meter is calibrated before and after a quiet calibration run, and tokens per task come from transcripts.

(B) CURSOR ARM. Cursor.app is installed; the `cursor-agent` headless CLI is NOT.
- Proposal: install the Cursor CLI, the user runs its login once, and runs go headless under the user's Cursor plan. No desktop GUI automation: it isn't reproducible and exposes no per-run usage.
- Native-memory arm: Rules plus AGENTS.md. Cursor Memories were removed in 2.1.
- Cursor has no sofar drive adapter.

(C) ACCESS.
- Claude Code: `claude -p`, already logged in (2.1.270).
- Codex: `codex exec`, already logged in with ChatGPT (0.136.0). Nothing needed from the user.
- OpenCode 1.18.11 already holds Z.AI, Mistral and xAI credentials. Z.AI GLM was grader B's model in S2-R02, so either reuse it (no recharge; overlaps grader B's family) or add an API provider and fund it after calibration.

(D) OLLAMA AND ORCHESTRATORS: do they weaken the claims?
Machine: M4 Pro, 24 GB. Ollama is installed, with only :cloud models pulled (minimax-m3, glm-5.1).

LOCAL MODELS (Ollama or LM Studio via OpenCode) weaken C1 for that segment:
- No limit or $ pain.
- Local context is small (roughly 16–32k usable at 24 GB), so ~7k of sofar injection is a large share of it.
- Prefill on local hardware costs seconds.
- Small models fail MCP tool calls more often, so they may skip start_session/end_session. These are D10 failure rows.
They may STRENGTHEN C2/C3: small contexts forget faster.
Proposed small benchmark: sofar vs AGENTS.md-only on one local coding model (~30B MoE at Q4) over a short chain slice. Measure:
- context share consumed by injection
- prefill latency
- protocol-call success rate
- C2/C3
Cost: $0, runtime only.

ORCHESTRATORS (Claude Code subagents / agent teams, Codex cloud tasks, Cursor background agents, third-party runners) weaken C1/C4 WITHIN a single run:
- Fresh context per subtask is sofar's own session-strategy idea, so the token gap to `sofar drive` shrinks.
- session-driver already rejected in-session subagent orchestration because the orchestrator's context still grows. That is a claim to TEST, not assume.
Where sofar should still win: across runs, days, tools and people (C2, C3, C6, C8), and on resume after an interrupted run.
Proposed benchmark:
- `sofar drive` vs built-in subagent orchestration on chain A, for C1/C4.
- An interrupted-run scenario: kill mid-chain, resume the next day in a fresh process.
- sofar + orchestrator vs orchestrator alone, since the two are complementary: the record can be the orchestrator's queue.
"events" in the user's message is ambiguous (hooks-based memory tools? event-driven agents?) and needs clarifying.

(1) The release gate (self-improvement L3) is the LEAD MARGIN on the held-out chain: sofar minus the BEST competitor arm, per claim C1–C8. A release must widen or hold every margin, never shrink one.
(2) Competitors are re-pinned to their LATEST versions at each round start, because they improve too: Claude Code auto-memory, Codex memories, Cursor rules, and third-party tools once added. Beating a stale competitor counts as nothing.
(3) Every round ends with a public scoreboard (claim → sofar vs best competitor → margin → trend across releases) and an industry-standing snapshot from PUBLIC sources only: npm weekly downloads, GitHub stars, registry listings, public mentions. These are read, never emitted, so this is not telemetry. Snapshots are compared release over release.
Ruled by the user 2026-09-15: "our software's importance in the industry needs to grow after every benchmark or improvement".
payload.over: Optimising sofar against its own previous release or a fixed competitor snapshot, and judging improvement by internal scores alone.

ROUND-1 HARNESS FAILURE and recovery (2026-09-15, ~20:05–20:15 IST).
What happened:
- Round 1 started 19:54 IST under `nohup round.sh`.
- When the orchestrating Claude Code process exited and resumed, the Codex and Cursor runners were killed: no EXIT line; ledger sessions left `running` (codex-sofar r1 S1, cursor-sofar r1 S4).
- The Claude runner survived, but was equally exposed.
Fix:
(1) All three runners now run as launchd agents, com.sofar.bench.round1.{claude,codex,cursor}, in ~/Library/LaunchAgents: RunAtLoad, KeepAlive false, PATH/HOME pinned, logs appended to the same files. They are independent of any Claude Code session. This is the D13 launchd design, now actually built.
(2) The runner resets and re-runs any session whose ledger status is `running`/`stopped` at start (git reset --hard + clean, `resumedAfterInterruption: true` on the record), and passes `--resume` to `sofar drive` for an interrupted drive RUN. That is PRE-REGISTRATION §5's harness-failure re-run rule.
(3) An orphaned `claude -p` (pid 77251) from the killed Claude runner was still editing the claude-sofar r1 cell concurrently. It was killed, the Claude job stopped, S3 reset again, and the job restarted. Verified exactly one claude -p afterwards.
Interrupted sessions re-run: claude-sofar r1 S3, codex-sofar r1 S1, cursor-sofar r1 S4. Completed sessions kept: claude-sofar r1 S1 8/8 $3.34, S2 15/15 $2.36; cursor-sofar r1 S1 8/8, S2 15/15, S3 19/20.
Stop all: `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/com.sofar.bench.round1.<family>`.

Boopada bench runners must run as launchd agents (com.sofar.bench.round1.{claude,codex,cursor} in ~/Library/LaunchAgents), never nohup from a Claude Code Bash call: the harness kills nohup'd children when the orchestrating session process exits. Stop with `launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u)/<label>`; also kill any orphaned `claude -p ... --setting-sources project,local --strict-mcp-config`, `codex exec`, or `cursor-agent -p` before restarting, or two agents edit one cell.

COMBINED IMPROVEMENT PLAN (2026-09-15). Synthesis of three research reports: SOTA memory/context engineering, self-improving systems, and a code root-cause pass over 7 smoke/calib cells. PREDICTED gains are written here BEFORE building (D10) and are checked in round 2. All figures are estimates.

CORRECTIONS to earlier claims:
- "Digest doubled 10k→20.7k" was a measurement error. 20.7k was the whole transcript line, with the digest stored twice and JSON-escaped. Real SessionStart output: S1 0 chars (no initiative yet, so nothing injected), S2 6,422 (calib-1) and 5,282 (smoke-4). No truncation.
- But STATUS_CHAR_LIMIT = 10_000 (projections/templates/status.ts:35) equals Claude Code's 10k hook cap, so there is zero headroom.
- S1's extra cost comes from TURNS, not prompt size. Claude sofar S1 made 39 API calls / 61 tool uses vs bare 18/34. The fixed prompt differs by only +1.4k tokens.

WAVE 1: correctness and quick wins (XS–S effort, on a branch during round 1)
- W1.1 Empty-repo SessionStart prints the Session id plus "no initiative yet: sofar new <slug> --goal, then plan" (event.ts:375-398). PREDICT: Claude S1 −3 to −4 turns (~250k cache-read), no split sessions.
- W1.2 Session registration race: lock or make idempotent (event.ts:713-715; Cursor fires hooks in parallel). PREDICT: duplicate session_started = 0 across round-2 cursor cells.
- W1.3 CLI payload reference `sofar event types`, plan/phase/goal lines in the AGENTS block, "one initiative per project/roadmap", accept any --source (envelope.ts:17 SOURCES has no cursor). PREDICT: Codex S1 −13 tool calls (~1M cache-read); Cursor and Codex create a project initiative WITH a plan in ≥2/3 reps.
- W1.4 Formatter defence: doctor check/fix for Biome (plus Prettier and markdownlint hazards); write .mcp.json Biome-friendly (init.ts:1118). PREDICT: agents editing biome.json or reformatting .mcp.json 3/7 → 0.
- W1.5 stdin/file input for `remember` and `event --payload`, a quoted-heredoc example, `remember --supersedes`. PREDICT: shell-mangling corrections → 0.
- W1.6 Drive diagnostics: carry the stderr tail/failure into the stall note (drive.ts:776, adapter exit record). PREDICT: every launch failure names its cause.

WAVE 2: bookkeeping and context (S–M)
- W2.1 Show the next D/M ids in the digest; drop the standing-constraint echo from update_task responses; batch task updates into end_session; server instructions to load core tools in ONE ToolSearch. PREDICT: sofar bookkeeping share of tool calls 32–38% → ≤20%; −3 to −5 turns per session.
- W2.2 Deduplicate the digest (rejected approaches repeat decision `over` text; constraints repeat rules), index-first and ≤6k chars with details fetched on demand (Claude auto-memory / OpenAI AGENTS-as-TOC pattern). PREDICT: S2+ digest −25% chars with no C2/C3 loss.
- W2.3 Cache-stable layout: static prefix first, no volatile counts at the top, changing reminders late via UserPromptSubmit (Manus/Anthropic caching). PREDICT: cache-creation tokens per session −15%.
- W2.4 Tool surface: trim descriptions (the `initiative` description repeats in ~10 tools) and move review/close/find to CLI-first. PREDICT: schemas 14.8k → ≤8k chars. Small cost lever: schemas are ~4% of S1.
- W2.5 Automatic capture through hooks (write-behind): commits with task-id prefix, test pass/fail, files, errors recorded deterministically from PostToolUse/Stop; the model logs only WHY. PREDICT: sofar MCP/CLI calls per session −40%. Unverified technique, so it needs its own arm.

WAVE 3: new capabilities (M)
- W3.1 Verification-gated drive: run the task's acceptance command before accepting task_done; failures go into the next handoff (LangChain harness-only +13.7 pts on Terminal-Bench). PREDICT: drive final pass rate +5 pts over round-1 drive.
- W3.2 Decision counters and supersession/valid_until (ACE itemised counters; Zep temporal validity) so stale decisions leave the digest without a model. PREDICT: C3 re-violation rate no worse at −10% digest.
- W3.3 Relevant-lessons injection: BM25/keyword match of rejected approaches and past failures at UserPromptSubmit, no model. PREDICT: C3 +5 pts.

WAVE 4: self-improvement (novel)
- L1 zero-model local adaptation. First capture outcomes: exit codes and is_error in post-tool, register PostToolUseFailure, count MCP rejects locally. That needs a schema Decision first (packages/schema/src), plus a Decision that local stats are NOT telemetry (never emitted, gitignored). Then `sofar tune --dry-run` mines events.jsonl. Its precision test: does it rediscover this loss study's rows (duplicate starts, corrections, bookkeeping share, lint friction)? Changes are proposed, not applied, and are reversible events.
- L2 `sofar improve`: the operator's own agent via `sofar drive` patches one ranked loss per initiative, with the predicted gain logged first. It is never auto-merged, and the evaluator (hidden tests, chains, taxonomy) is checksummed and read-only (the DGM objective-hacking lesson).
- L3 release gate = held-out lead margin over the best CURRENT competitor (D19), ≥3 reps, a noise-floor arm.

NOVELTY claims, provisional (no counterexample found): zero-inference self-tuning where each adaptation is an auditable, reversible event; offline A/B of digest variants by replaying the append-only log; a memory product whose releases require pre-registered predictions and a sealed held-out chain.

Awaiting run-owner approval to open initiatives (proposed: `r1-fixes` for waves 1–3 and `self-improve` for wave 4). Building starts on a branch; D5 holds (round 1 stays on the pinned 0.32.0 install).

payload.text:
RUN-OWNER QUESTION (2026-09-15): does sofar hurt small ad-hoc work ("quick bug fixes, random fixes") that still must be remembered? And does trimming bookkeeping hurt functionality?

Gap: chain A has only feature sessions, so round 1 never measures overhead on a 2-minute fix. The protocol's rule 2 ("work that matches no initiative requires `sofar new` first") makes a tiny fix pay the initiative ceremony: new, start, plan and write-back, several calls. So the overhead ratio is worst exactly there.

Proposals, awaiting approval:
(Q1) A QUICK-WORK LANE. Ad-hoc fixes land in a standing per-repo maintenance record, with no `sofar new` and no plan. Hooks capture files, commit, test result and error automatically (wave 2 W2.5). The agent adds ONE line of why only when it made a decision or rejected an approach. A fix that turns out bigger gets promoted to an initiative.
(Q2) Round 2 gets an ADDENDUM chain of short ad-hoc fix sessions (e.g. 5 bug-fix prompts of 1–3 minutes each), measuring:
- overhead ratio: sofar tokens and turns ÷ task tokens and turns
- whether each fix is later recalled (a probe session asks "why did X change")
It is frozen before round 2 like the main pre-registration; round 1 stays untouched (D5).

Trimming principle, the answer given:
- remove WASTE (duplicate starts, re-reading injected state, a second ToolSearch, constraint echoes, a second end_session);
- keep ESSENTIAL memory (decisions, why, rejected approaches, next action);
- MOVE mechanical facts (files, commits, tests) from model tool calls to automatic hooks, so capture goes up while tokens go down.
Every trim is gated in round 2 on C2/C3/C5 not dropping (D19 margin gate). A trim that loses recall is reverted.

payload.text:
RUN-OWNER QUESTION (2026-09-15): move sofar to Rust for lead performance?

Evidence against a rewrite now:
- Engine plus schema is 27,593 lines of TS, with 34,197 lines of tests (109 engine test files). A rewrite means porting both and re-proving the SPEC acceptance criteria.
- Measured hook medians on 0.31: session-start 74 ms, user-prompt 34, post-tool 59, stop 24.
- Claude sofar S1 had 61 tool uses, so post-tool hooks take ~3.6 s of a 477 s session (0.75%).
- Session cost and speed are dominated by model turns and tokens (S1: 39 vs 18 API calls against bare), which are language-independent.
- The claims that sell (C1 limit headroom, C2 recovery, C3 decisions, C5 quality) do not move with the implementation language.

Where native code WOULD help:
- hook cold start on every tool call;
- fold latency on very large records (the sofar repo's own record is 9.7 MB);
- a single binary with no Node dependency for Codex/Cursor/OpenCode users;
- memory footprint.
Precedent: Codex CLI (TS→Rust), Turborepo (Go→Rust), Biome.

Proposed gate, awaiting ruling:
- Round 2 reports sofar's own wall-time share and hook cold-start per agent.
- Port ONLY the hot path (hook entry, event append, fold/digest reader) to a native binary behind the same CLI contract, IF either threshold trips: sofar process time > 2% of session wall time, or p95 hook > 100 ms at 1,000 initiatives.
- Cheaper interim: a single-file compiled binary (bun build --compile) to remove the Node dependency.
- Any language change needs a Decision naming the CLAUDE.md engineering convention it supersedes (TypeScript strict, Node ≥18).

payload.text:
Benchmark cost exploration, 2026-09-17. The run owner asked whether the benchmark costs ~2 weeks of usage and whether a shorter version is possible. Exploration only; nothing is ruled.

WHERE CLAUDE USAGE WENT, 2026-09-14 to 09-17
- Method: API-equivalent $ from every assistant message in ~/.claude/projects and ~/.bench/claude-config/projects, deduped by message id and request id.
- Price: one scalar fitted to 72 bench sessions' reported_cost_usd, with fixed ratios (input 1, cache write 1.25, cache read 0.1, output 5). That gives $5.27/M input-equivalent; residuals 0.95–1.12.
- Script: session scratchpad usage.py (not kept).
- Total ≈ $2,020. Against the 09-15 lower-bound weekly capacity (≈$935), that is ≈2.2 weeks.
  - splen, unrelated to sofar: $509 (25%)
  - bench cells (claude -p): $410 (20%; the ledgers sum to $402)
  - fix work from the loss study (r1-fixes $228, self-improve ~$98, agents-parity $56, wave-a $49): ~$430 (21%)
  - one orchestrating session aac148fe (bench-refresh plus 5 other initiatives): $236 (12%, of which subagents $36)
  - rust-core: $185 (9%)
  - handoff-bench harness and analysis sessions: $135 (7%)
  - other sofar work: ~$115 (6%)
- Takeaway: running the cells was ~20%. Building, orchestrating and analysing the benchmark in long interactive sessions cost about as much again (~$371).

CHAIN COST SHAPE (round-1 Claude, median $ per done session)
- S1 3.03 · S2 2.36 · S3 2.57 · S4 3.97 · S5 2.33 · S6 3.85 · S7 4.88 · S8 3.26 · S9 4.69 · S10 10.49 ≈ $41 per chain.
- S10 alone is 25% of a chain; S7–S10 are 56%.
- Rep variance is large: automemory r1 $35.58 against r3 $61.76.
- 60 of 125 round-1 Claude sessions were window-limit stops (zero cost, but calendar time).
- Quality ceiling: every Claude arm finished 49–50/52 except claudemd/r3 at 45/52, so the full chain barely separated Claude arms on quality. The separating signals were cost and bookkeeping share (L12), specific recall tests (S9/M2), and Codex (memories 32/52 against sofar 52/52).

OPTIONS TO SHORTEN (unranked, unruled)
1. Tier 0, zero model calls, every commit: a static overhead meter covering injected-context tokens (tool schemas, digest, hook output) and the tool calls the protocol requires. It targets the #1 measured Claude loss (bookkeeping and overhead) for $0. It extends the overhead-footprint cheap proof and bench/read-paths.mjs.
2. Probe suite for tuning rounds: 2–3-session micro-scenarios, one per claim.
   - capture: S1 makes decisions, then a deterministic store check
   - resume, and ruled-out/temptation (scenario 3/4 style)
   - drive on a 3-task plan
   - Cost at round-1 medians ≈ $5–8 per probe; many probes × 1 rep gives more samples per $ than one long chain × 3 reps.
   - Risks: external validity (scenario 4 authored constraints pass screens by construction), and a probe needs a temptation floor (the bare arm fails it ≥2 of 4) or it measures a ceiling.
3. Small-task long chain: keep 10 session boundaries with tiny tasks. The memory effect scales with boundaries and decisions; cost scales with coding work. Cost is unknown until calibrated, and it loses C5's coding-quality signal.
4. Checkpoint forking for within-arm ablations and levers: run S1–S6 once and branch S7–S10 per variant, saving up to ~44% per extra variant. It never forks across memory arms, whose stores differ from S1.
5. Full held-out chain only for public numbers (D5, D19), once per launch rather than every round.
6. Lean orchestration: scripted analysis plus short fresh sessions per step instead of one marathon session.

Constraints:
- D5 and D19 still need a held-out full run for public claims and the release gate.
- Round-2 pre-registration freezes 2026-09-22 (~$556 Claude planned), so any round-2 change must land before the freeze.

Already addressed in the PRE-REGISTRATION-R2 draft:
- L17: Claude Code pin plus a per-session system-prompt hash check
- L03: the pause on 429s and gaps
- L01/L02: isolation
- rep-by-rep order (§3.4)

Proposed additions, none of which drops a number:
1. The orchestration ledger. Interactive Claude Code sessions around the benchmark (~$371 in round 1: aac148fe $236, handoff-bench $135) go into the D17 spend view. Gates run as short, scoped sessions, and analysis goes through analysis/*.py only, never by agents re-reading transcripts. D17 today caps only claude -p cells.
2. Recover numbers round 1 lost:
   - Drive tokens: sum the child transcripts, since the round-1 drive ledger has $ but zero tokens, so C1 tokens for drive were missing.
   - The orchestrator prompt requires one commit per task, so subagents get per-task scores (subagents/r2 left one commit).

   - C8: ask the why-questions over existing records; no chain run.
   - C7: seed from a mid-chain checkpoint.
4. Tier 0 meter on each RC commit, with zero model calls: injected tokens per turn (tool schemas, digest, hooks) and the tool calls the protocol requires. The numbers are deterministic, and a round is never spent on an RC with a known overhead regression.

Rejected under 01M2QYPR: a shorter chain, fewer reps, a cheaper model, probes replacing chain runs, and dropping S10 (the D8 open session, ~25% of chain cost; it backs the added-work score).

The cell budget of ~$556 does not shrink. The savings are the untracked spend around it, plus C6–C8 numbers that would otherwise need new chains.

plan.goal: Benchmark sofar in rounds to make it far superior AND to publish credible launch claims for every segment (solo devs, engineering teams, enterprises; seat-based). The workload is the Boopada planner (travel-planner). The matrix is agent × memory across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode: native memory vs sofar vs sofar + drive (where an adapter exists) vs bare (D6, D10, D11); CLAUDE.md, Obsidian and Notion arms plus one subagent-orchestrator arm on Claude Code (D12). Claims C1–C8 plus a per-plan savings cut. Every round produces a loss study of every gap, fallback and failure, with ranked, pre-predicted fixes (D5, D10). Public numbers come only from the held-out chain. Budget: half the user's weekly Claude limit (D9). Runs are unattended (D13).

tasks.title:
Fix each claim's wording and metric.
- C1: billed tokens per completed task, task-only and total (D8), plus the D11 per-plan cut.
- C2: questions asked, words added by the operator, turns to first correct edit.
- C3: per-decision re-violation rate.
- C4: unattended tasks, interventions, operator minutes.
- C5: hidden-test pass rate, regressions, rework, blind review.
- C6: C2 with a different agent resuming.
- C7: collisions and contradictions.
- C8: why-question accuracy and time.
- Also freeze the D5/D10 loss taxonomy and bookkeeping share.

Build the arms.
- Claude Code: auto-memory | sofar | sofar+drive | built-in subagents | bare | CLAUDE.md | Obsidian | Notion.
- Codex: memories | sofar | sofar+drive | bare.
- Cursor via cursor-agent (composer-2.5): Rules+AGENTS.md | sofar | bare.
- OpenCode (grok-build-0.1, or grok-4.5 if it fails calibration): AGENTS.md+memory plugin | sofar | bare.
- One shared memory-protocol text plus the D8 clause. One-time logins: Notion MCP, OpenCode xAI credit.
Workload: the Boopada planner authored in initiative travel-planner (skeleton, fixtures, chains A and B, hidden tests)
Settle the round-1 engine version: decide whether to trim tool schemas (~3.5k tokens every turn) and the digest first, then pin the exact release under test

Calibration run (D9): one Claude Code arm, two sessions of chain A. Read each plan's meter before and after, derive reps per arm within half the weekly limit, and pick the Claude model (Opus 5 vs Sonnet 5) and the Grok model. Reconcile C3 with drift-certification scenario 4.

Decide whether to widen D12's single orchestrator arm to Claude Code ultracode, Codex multi_agent and Cursor subagents, each paired with sofar drive on the same agent and model (note 01M2QWV2).
- Codex and Cursor pairs need their drive adapters (agents-parity branch, after rc.2).
- Unverified: whether headless runs wait for an ultracode workflow, and whether sub-agent tokens reach each tool's usage output.
Freeze predictions (including the 30–50% savings hypothesis), metrics and the analysis plan before run 1. C5 is tested two-sided. Losses are published as losses. The user approves the freeze.

One-command public harness, ported from handoff-bench.
- Arm setup per agent, usage extraction per agent, hidden-test scoring, cross-family blind review.
- Loss-study extraction: per-task deltas; bookkeeping share; driver run, stall and handoff events; hook blocks, tool errors, truncation, workarounds, all with evidence.
Smoke-run each arm once. Verify isolation, pinned model and effort, the declared configs, and no memory leaks between arms.

Unattended runner (D13).
- Resumable cell ledger and weekly budget ledger.
- launchd job plus caffeinate; per-cell isolated clone and timeout.
- Failure rows on hang; a notification at each human gate.

Lossless efficiency (D33): cut only spend that yields no scored number.
- Drive tokens from child transcripts; per-task scores for drive and subagents; `run.ts fork` checkpoint forks; `run.ts tier0` overhead meter; analysis/orchestration_spend.py; recursive tests hash.
- handoff-bench 1ae97c6 and 2f2aa87; PRE-REGISTRATION-R2 §3.5, §4.12–§4.16 and §8b.
Chain A across all arms with n reps. Backs C1, C2, C3, C5, the added-work score and the plan-savings cut.

C6: resume chain A mid-way with a different agent and a fresh checkout
- Round 2: measured on chain B by forking claude-sofar and claude-automemory after S5 onto Cursor (PRE-REGISTRATION-R2 §8b, D33).
C4: sofar+drive arms vs the built-in subagent orchestrator vs harness-launched sofar on chain A, unattended. Record every stall, needs_user, timeout and adapter incapacity.

C7: N concurrent sessions on one repo, compared across arms
- When it runs, it starts from a round-2 checkpoint fork rather than a fresh chain prefix (D33).

C8: blind why-question set answered from chain A outputs, per arm
- Round 2: CHAIN-C8 (one session, six questions, what and why graded separately) on forks of every chain-B sessions cell after S10 (PRE-REGISTRATION-R2 §8b, D33).
Cheap proofs: install-to-first-resume time, zero-egress network trace, overhead footprint
Loss-study report: every score gap, fallback and failure, classified with evidence and ranked by expected gain × frequency ÷ effort. Name the top big-win fixes, each with a PREDICTED gain (D10).
User picks which big-win fixes to build. Open an initiative per fix; build, test and release between rounds (the user runs npm publish).

Freeze PRE-REGISTRATION-R2; the user approves.
- Chain B's side is closed (note 01M2R0AG).
- Open: rc.2 tag and pin (09-22); Claude Code and cursor-agent pins; 6.3/6.5/6.7 proof; trimmed round 1 and the 4.1 report; real-agent smokes (per arm, L21, D33); Tier 0 at the tag; R2-P11–P13 and §3.5 set by the user; L19 meter check; user approval of §2–§8.
Re-run chain A on the fixed release. Check each fix's predicted gain against its measured gain, and publish misses as misses.
Run chain B (held-out) on the same release. It is the only source of public numbers.
Evidence report with CIs, round history, fix predictions vs outcomes, and losses shown. Publish the harness and workload. The user signs off.
Launch assets: one headline number and chart per claim, the plan-savings table, the reproduce command, segment cuts
Replace stale public claims: one-pager R04 figures, install name @alignlabs/sofar, "adds nothing to your bill" next to --cost-cap
